(Family Letter No. 4)
Tokyo
Tuesday, February 7, 1950
Dear Family,
On Saturday, February 4 Amos Hiatt of PAA, who is
helping me on the Tokyo deal, and I drove down to Kobe with -
of all things - two Turks.
An uncle and his nephew.
The
former hes a history which is tragic.
He was born in a little
town on the Amur River in Manchuria where his father was a
wealthy merchant dealing in wool and furs. In 1920 the Russian
Reds killed his father.
The mother escaped down the Amur in
small boat with her eight children, was picked up at sea by
a Japanese gunboat and brought to Kobe. There the children
got along on next to nothing but survived.

old firm whichhad been taken over by some Jews.
Later he went
into business for himself out in Sinkiang Province and ran a
fleet of trucks along the old silk road from Peiping across
the Gobi Desert to Hami, Turfan and throughout northwestern
China.
He made quite a fortune.
He had to drop everything
when the Communists took over in China. Now his wife is in
Peiping while he
is staying in Kobe with his sister who is
married to another wealthy Turk. It was the sister's son who
drove the car - a Plymouth. The boy is very good-looking. He
has lived all his nineteen years in Japan - speaks English like
an American and Japanese like a Japanese.
We started out at 5:00 a.m. in the dark, skirting
Yokohama and going on to the Fugia Hotel at Menoshita
breakfast. Leaving there we had our first view of Fuji which,
through the morning haze, looked as red as it is depicted on
the Japanese painted pillow covers which the sailors buy in
Panama.
Later it was gold color.
We stopped at Lake Hakone
where our host, the uncle, took some color films which I hope
to bring home to show you all. We drove all day through little
Japanese villages and open country over roads sometimes good
but often in bad shape.

town next to e small sawmill. The owner brought us out three
chairs and we had lunch - beer, sandwiches and fried chicken

so good. However, Frederick told me rather proudly that his
father spoke Russian, French, German, Turkish, Chinese and
Japanese fluently.
Four buildings which he owned had been
destroyed by American bombing raids during the war.
Sunday we
went to see the femous Takarazuka girls
The theatre is owned by the PAA agents in Osaka who
also put on the show.
The play was a Japanese version of
Romeo and Juliet, in
which all the players were girls.
ending was a new
version which might or might not appeal to
William Shakespeare.
After the scene where Romeo dies of
poison and Juliet kills herself, the curtain came down and
the "Takarazuka Ballet", a copy of the "Rockettes" danced

I sat next to the President and could hardly
keep from laughing at the wrong time.
Presently the "Rockettes"
made their ponderous way off the stage and the curtain rose on
a scene in the clouds where Romeo and Juliet, complete with tin
halos, climb hand in hand up to heaven.
We went backstage with
the President and he lined up the entire cast to make a photo-
graph of us in heaven!
We drove back to our host's for a Turkish dinner
which I can't describe and do not know what I ate, but
everything was good.
Monday we spent with our agents in Osaka and Kobe
and had dinner at the home of the President whose wife waited
on table - a rare but very gracious gesture.
At 9:00 p.m. we took the express train back to
Tokyo, arriving here at 7:30 this morning.
The other day a friend presented me with the fol-
lowing piece which will appeal to the older ones of you more
than the younger:
HOW TO GUESS YOUR AGE
y Corey For
"It seems to me that they are building staircases
steeper than they used to.
The risers are higher, or they are
making more of them, or semething. Maybe this is because it is
so much farther today from the first floor to the second floor,
but I've noticed it is getting harder to make two steps at a
time any more. Nowadays it is all I can do to make one step at
a time.
Another thing I've noticed is the small print they're
using lately. Newspapers are getting ferther and farther away
when I hold them, and I have to squint to make them out.
other day I had
to back halfway out of a telephone booth in order

-3-
to read the number on the coin box. It is obviously ridi-
culous to suggest that a person my age needs glasses, but the
only other way I can find out whet's going on is to have some-
body read aloud to me, and that's not too satisfactory because
no, no hasis not
people speak in such a low voice these days I can't hear them
very well.
Everything is farther than it used to be. It's twice
the distance from
my
house to the station now, and they've added
a fair-sized hill that I never noticed before.
The trains leave
sooner, too.
I've given up running for them, because they start
faster
these days when I try to catch them.
You can't depend on timetables any more, and it's no
use asking the conductor. I ask him a dozen times a trip if the
next station is where I get off, and he always seys it isn't.
How can you trust a conductor like that?
Usually I gather up
my bundles and stand in the aisle a couple of stops away just
to make sure I don't go past my destination. Sometimes I make
double sure by getting off at the station ahead.
A lot of other things
are different lately.
Barbers
no longer hold up a mirror behind me when they've finished, so
I can see the back of my head, and my wife has been taking
care
of the tickets lately when we go to the theatre.
They don't
put the same material into clothes any more either.
I've noticed
that all my suits have a tendency to shrink, especially in certain
places such as around the waist, or in the seat of the pants, and
the laces they put in shoes nowadays are much harder to reach.
Even the weather is changing.
It's getting colder in
the winter, and the summers are hotter than they used
to be. I'd
go away, if it wasn't so far.
Snow is heavier when I try to
shovel it, and I have to put on rubbers whenever I go out, because
rain today is wetter then the rain we used to get. Drafts are
more severe, too. It must be the way they build windows now.
People are changing, too.
For one thing, they're
younger than they used to be when I was their age.
I went back
recently to an alumni reunion at the College I graduated from in
1943-that is, 1933 - I mean 1923 - and I wes shocked to see the
mere tots they're admitting as students these days.
The average
age of the Freshman Class couldn't have been more than 7.
They
seem to be more polite than in my time, though; several under-
graduates called me "Sir" and one of them asked me if he could
help me across the street.
On the other hand, people my own age are so much
older than I am.
I realize that my generetion is approaching
middle age; (I define middle age roughly as the period between
21 and 110), but there is no excuse for my classmates tottering
into a state of senility.
I ran into my old roommate at the bar,
and he'd changed so much that he didn't recognize me.
"You've put on a little weight, George", I said.

-4-
"It's this modern food", George said. "It seems to
be more fattening."
"How about another Martini?" I said. "Have you
noticed how much weaker the Martinis are these days?"
"Everything is different," said George. "Even
the food you get. It's more fattening."
"How long since I've seen you, George?" I said, "It
must be several years."
"I think the last time was right after the election",
seid George.
"What election was that?"
George thought for a moment.
"Coolidge," he said. I
ordered a couple more Martinis.
"Have you noticed these Mar-
tinis are weaker than they used to be?" I said.
"It isn't like the good old days, " George said. Re-
member when we'd go down to the Speak, and order
some Orange
Blossoms, and maybe pick up a couple of Flappers? Boy, could
they neck! Hot Diggety!"
"You used to be quite a ceke-eater, George, " I said.
"Do you still do the Bleck Bottom?"
"I put on too much weight," said George.
"This food
nowadays seems to be more fattening." "I know," I said, "you
mentioned that just a minute ago."
"Did I?" said George, "How about another Martini?" I
said.
"Have you noticed that the Martinis aren't as strong as
they used to be?"
"Yeah, " said George, "you said that twice before."
"Oh," I said . . . • •
•
I got to thinking about poor old George when I was
shaving this morning.
I stopped for a moment and looked at my
own reflection in the mirror, They don't seem to use the same
kind of glass in mirrors any more.
*
*
*
Still expect Debby and Hebe to arrive Tokyo on the
17th and take off with them right away for Honolulu.
As ever,
н. м. В.
